entities.name: Behaviours suggestive of anxiety during owner absence
Video recording with focal animal continuous sampling

relationships.evidenceLevel: Low — significant but moderate correlation, rs = 0.438, P = 0.003, n=31 dogs, single 25-minute recording each
Low — owner-report/video correlations were higher for more apparent behaviours such as destruction than for subtler signs
Low — video was the reference measure here, but a single session cannot separate habitual pattern from day-specific behaviour
Low — implied by the moderate correlation and the stronger performance on evidence-leaving behaviours; not directly quantified
Very Low — some dogs were recorded with conspecifics present; the design was not powered to disentangle this

aiAgentFacts.fact: Owner C-BARQ separation-related behaviour scores showed a significant moderate positive correlation with the percentage of time dogs spent in anxiety-suggestive behaviours on video (rs = 0.438, P = 0.003, n = 31).
A similar moderate correlation held against the first principal component of recorded behaviours (rs = 0.385, P = 0.008).
Correlations between owner report and video were higher for more apparent behaviours such as destruction — owners read best the behaviours that leave physical evidence.
Behaviour was recorded during the first 25 minutes after the owner's departure using focal animal continuous sampling.
A correlation of 0.438 supports neither 'owners know' nor 'owners have no idea' — owner report carries real signal and substantial error simultaneously.
The authors state that further work with more participants and repeated recordings is required before their conclusion can be relied upon.
The study establishes a group-level correlation; it does not identify which individual owners are accurate, nor validate any individual owner's impression.

historyQuestions: Not prescribed by this paper. Its signal asymmetry finding does support treating owner reports of visible aftermath (destruction, toileting) as better-grounded than owner reports of subtle in-absence distress, and supports requesting video where available.
redFlags: Not addressed — this study identifies no red-flag findings and defines no urgency threshold.
differentialDiagnosesMentioned: Not addressed — the study validates a questionnaire against video and does not evaluate medical causes such as pain or cognitive decline that can mimic or contribute to separation-related behaviour.
recommendedDiagnosticWorkups: Video recording of the dog during owner absence, coded by continuous sampling, served as the study's reference measure — interpretation requires a veterinarian or qualified behaviourist.

limitations: Small sample: 31 dogs, each recorded once — day-to-day variation and camera novelty cannot be separated from habitual behaviour
Single 25-minute window immediately post-departure; nothing is established about behaviour across a full working day
Moderate correlation (rs = 0.438) leaves substantial unexplained variance; the result must not be reported as owners being either reliable or unreliable
Some dogs were recorded with one or two conspecifics present, an uncontrolled source of variation in this design
Group-level correlation only — no way to identify which individual owners' reports are trustworthy
Medical differentials for separation-related behaviour, including pain and canine cognitive dysfunction, were outside the study's scope
